t.3.17.1: Then Rāma, smiling first, spoke in a clear and gentle voice to that Śūrpaṇakhā, who was bound fast by the noose of desire.
t.3.17.3: But this is my younger brother, virtuous and pleasing to behold, glorious and valiant, Lakṣmaṇa by name, who has not taken a wife.
t.3.17.2: I am already married; this is my beloved wife. For women such as you, sharing a husband with a co-wife would be a source of great sorrow.
t.3.17.5: O large-eyed one, accept this brother of mine as your husband; O lady of lovely hips, without any co-wife, attend upon him as the radiance of the sun attends upon Mount Meru.
t.3.17.4: He has never had a wife before and is eager for one; he is young and pleasing to look upon, and he will be a husband for you well matched to this beauty of yours.
t.3.17.6: Thus addressed by Rāma, the rākṣasī, deluded by desire, abruptly left Rāma and then spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
t.3.17.7: I, a woman of excellent complexion, am a wife fit for this form of yours; with me you will roam happily through all the Daṇḍaka forests.
t.3.17.8: Thus addressed by the rākṣasī, Saumitri Lakṣmaṇa, skilled in speech, smiled and then spoke these fitting words to Śūrpaṇakhā.
t.3.17.9: How can you wish to become the wife of a slave like me, and thus a slave yourself? I am dependent on my noble brother, O you whose complexion is like the lotus.
t.3.17.10: O large-eyed one, become the younger wife of my noble brother, whose fortunes are abundant; so shall your aims be fulfilled, and you will be joyful and of spotless complexion.
t.3.17.11: Casting off this misshapen, unchaste, hideous, hollow-bellied, aged wife, he will devote himself to you alone.
t.3.17.12: For what discerning man, O fair-complexioned one, having abandoned this most excellent beauty, would set his heart upon mere humans, O lady of lovely hips?
t.3.17.13: Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, she, the hideous one with the sagging belly, unskilled in recognizing jest, took those words to be true.
t.3.17.14: Deluded by desire, she spoke to Rāma, the invincible scorcher of foes, who was seated in the leaf-hut together with Sītā.
t.3.17.16: Today, while you look on, I shall devour this human woman, and then, free of any rival, I shall roam with you as I please.
t.3.17.15: Clinging to this misshapen, unchaste, hideous, hollow-bellied, aged wife, you do not think much of me.
t.3.17.17: Having spoken thus, she whose eyes were like firebrands, utterly enraged, rushed at the fawn-eyed lady, like a great meteor rushing upon Rohiṇī.
t.3.17.18: As she came rushing at him like the noose of Death, the mighty Rāma checked her; then, enraged, he spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
t.3.17.19: O Saumitri, one should never in any way jest with cruel and ignoble beings. Look, gentle one, Vaidehī is barely alive.
t.3.17.20: O tiger among men, you should disfigure this hideous, unchaste, wildly frenzied, pot-bellied rākṣasī.
t.3.17.21: Thus addressed, the mighty Lakṣmaṇa, enraged, drew his sword and, while Rāma looked on, cut off her ears and nose.
t.3.17.22: Her ears and nose cut off, the dreadful Śūrpaṇakhā, having let out a discordant howl, fled into the forest by the way she had come.
t.3.17.23: That disfigured, exceedingly dreadful rākṣasī, drenched in blood, roared many kinds of roars, like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season.
t.3.17.24: She, dreadful to behold, streaming blood in many places, raised her arms and, roaring, entered the great forest.
t.3.17.25: Then she, disfigured, approached her brother Khara of fierce energy, who was dwelling in Janasthāna surrounded by hosts of rākṣasas, and fell to the ground like a thunderbolt falling from the sky.
t.3.17.26: Then she, the sister of Khara, stupefied by fear and confusion and drenched in blood, told him everything: that Rāghava had come to the forest with his wife and with Lakṣmaṇa, and of the disfigurement done to her own person.
